summary: Documents an already deployed RADIUS extension in which a client can query whether a RADIUS server is working, using the Status-Server packet code that RFC 2865 reserved for experimental use. It is informational and not an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Status-Server lets a RADIUS client ask a directly connected server whether it is responding, without pretending that a user is logging in. The request must include Message-Authenticator, and proxies do not forward it.

subtitle: A RADIUS message for checking a server without sending a login or accounting request.

tldr.problem: A RADIUS client may not know whether a silent server is down. Using a login or accounting request as a probe can trigger user-authentication or accounting side effects.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a Status-Server packet with Code 12 and a required Message-Authenticator. The server replies with Access-Accept on the authentication port or Accounting-Response on the accounting port; proxies do not forward the query.
tldr.outcome: The hop-by-hop query can help a client decide whether to fail over. RFC 5997 is Informational and updates RFC 2866.

sections.title: Why Status-Server Is Separate
sections.content:
Status-Server uses the RADIUS Code 12, which RFC 2865 had reserved for experimental use. The extension lets a client query a server's status and is stateless; a query should not affect normal server operation beyond possibly changing a packet counter.

An Access-Request can look like a real login and may trigger challenges, rejects, alerts, delays, or local policy actions. An Accounting-Request can look like a real accounting event and may put false information in an accounting database. The RFC recommends against sending either type solely as a liveness check.
sections.plainLanguage: A purpose-built status request avoids making a server treat a probe as a user login or accounting event. It checks one server directly and does not travel through a proxy.

sections.title: Packet Format and Replies
sections.content:
A Status-Server request uses the RADIUS packet format and includes a 16-octet Request Authenticator. It must also include the Message-Authenticator attribute, which provides per-packet authentication and integrity protection. A server must send no more than one response.

A query to the authentication port receives an Access-Accept; a query to the accounting port receives an Accounting-Response. The request packet format is the same for both ports. The response authenticator is calculated using the request authenticator and shared secret.
sections.plainLanguage: The request includes a random authenticator and a required message check. The reply type depends on whether the client queried the authentication or accounting port.

sections.title: Client, Server and Proxy Behavior
sections.content:
Clients should let administrators enable or disable Status-Server globally and per server; the default is disabled. A client must not retransmit a Status-Server packet. To try again, it sends a new packet with a new identifier and authenticator. Servers should allow administrators to control whether they accept these packets.

A server must discard requests from unknown clients or requests with an invalid Message-Authenticator. A proxy must not forward Status-Server, so the answer reports only on the directly addressed server. A client can use repeated checks to detect when a previously unresponsive server responds again.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a fresh status request for each attempt rather than retransmitting an old one. A proxy does not pass the request onward, so the result is about the server that received it.

sections.title: Limits and Security
sections.content:
Status-Server can show whether a directly addressed server responds, but not whether that server can reach a particular realm behind it. RFC 5997 recommends combining status checks with failover; realm routing and destination-unreachable signaling are outside its scope.

Without Message-Authenticator enforcement, an attacker could spoof requests, cause reflected denial-of-service traffic, or race a valid request and prompt an Access-Accept. The RFC says implementations that fail to require Message-Authenticator are not recommended. It also notes that RADIUS uses MD5 for packet authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: A reply confirms that the queried server responded, not that every destination behind it is reachable. The message authenticator is essential because unauthenticated status requests can be forged.
